14.3.4.3 Iron as Catalyst in Reaction between Persulphate and Iodide Ions

The reaction between persulphate ions (peroxodisulphate ions), S₂O₈²⁻, and iodide ions in solution can be catalysed using either iron (II) or iron (III) ions. The overall equation for the reaction is,

S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂

The catalyst used in this reaction is iron (II) ions. This reaction occurs in two steps.

S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺

2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂

If you use iron (III) ions, the second of these reactions happens first.

14.3.4.4 Reactions of Hexaaquairon (II) and Hexaaquairon(III) with Water and Ammonia

Reactions of Hexaaquairon (II) with Water

Many hexaaqua complex ions can undergo acid base reactions with water to produce a solution of pH less than seven. These are not redox reactions because during the reaction no change in the oxidation state of central metal occurs e.g.

[Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]⁺ + H₃O⁺

Reactions of Hexaaquairon (II) with Ammonia

Ammonia can act as both a base and a ligand. In these cases, it simply acts as a base – removing hydrogen ions from the aqua complex.

[Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2NH₃ → [Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂] + 2NH₄⁺

Reactions of Hexaaquairon (III) with Water

In iron (III) case,

[Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + H₂O(l) ⇌ [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺ + H₃O⁺

Fe³⁺ (ferric) gives more acidic solution than Fe²⁺ (ferrous) ions.

Reactions of Hexaaquairon (III) with Ammonia

In Fe(III) case

[Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + 3NH₃ → [Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃] + 3NH₄⁺

However, breaking the nitrogen triple bond to form N₂H₂ is very difficult and resulting compound is highly unstable and is likely to dissociate as soon as it is formed. The formation of N₂H₂ is highly endothermic. So the above reactions do not proceed easily without the use of catalyst.

The hydrogen and nitrogen are adsorbed on metallic iron surface.

N₂(g) ⇌ N₂(ad)

The hydrogen almost immediately splits into its component atoms by sharing or exchange of electrons with the catalyst surface.

H₂(g) ⇌ 2H(ad)

The nitrogen molecules split into their component atoms and they lock into the surface of the iron catalyst. This is the slowest step and so limits the rate of the entire process.

N₂(ad) ⇌ 2N(ad)

The hydrogen atoms migrate across the surface of the catalyst and react with nitrogen and produce ammonia molecules that are still bound to the surface.

N(ad) + H(ad) → NH(ad)

NH(ad) + H(ad) → NH₂(ad)

NH₂(ad) + H(ad) → NH₃(ad)

The assembled ammonia molecules are desorbed from surface in the form of gas

NH₃(ad) ⇌ NH₃(g)

Figure 14.8 Catalytic action of iron surface in Haber process.

14.3.4.3 Iron as Catalyst in Reaction between Persulphate and Iodide Ions

The reaction between persulphate ions (peroxodisulphate ions), S₂O₈²⁻, and iodide ions in solution can be catalysed using either iron (II) or iron (III) ions. The overall equation for the reaction is,

S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂

The catalyst used in this reaction is iron (II) ions. This reaction occurs in two steps.

S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺

2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂

If you use iron (III) ions, the second of these reactions happens first.

14.3.4.4 Reactions of Hexaaquairon (II) and Hexaaquairon(III) with Water and Ammonia

Reactions of Hexaaquairon (II) with Water

Many hexaaqua complex ions can undergo acid base reactions with water to produce a solution of pH less than seven. These are not redox reactions because during the reaction no change in the oxidation state of central metal occurs e.g.

[Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]⁺ + H₃O⁺

Reactions of Hexaaquairon (II) with Ammonia

Ammonia can act as both a base and a ligand. In these cases, it simply acts as a base – removing hydrogen ions from the aqua complex.

[Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2NH₃ → [Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂] + 2NH₄⁺
